newsitem.title: POLAND: THOUSANDS EVACUATED DESPITE POLISH FLOOD'S RETREAT.
newsitem.headline: THOUSANDS EVACUATED DESPITE POLISH FLOOD'S RETREAT.

text.p: More than 15,000 thousand people were evacuated on Sunday from the town of Slubice, on the German border, as the swelling Odra river threatened to swamp the area, but the flood receded in other regions of southwestern Poland.

The evacuation came just as Polish Interior Minister Leszek Miller met his German counterpart Manfred Kanther in Slubice, accross the river from Frankfurt an der Oder, to discuss coordination of efforts to combat the disaster.
"We are evacuating people from Slubice as a precaution. The level of Odra is 12 cm higher than in 1930 when a great flood took place," said crisis committee spokesman Krzysztof Pomes.

Local flood committee spokeswoman Lidia Markindorf said the town, situated in a low-laying area, could be hit be a huge flood surge any time if the eroded and sodden protection dykes burst despite frantic sand-bagging.
"The situation in Slubice is dangerous. We have seen the Odra's level increasing by 40 cm...and dykes are soaked," private Radio Zet quoted Markindorf as saying.
Radio Zet reported that those who refused to be evacuated from Slubice had to sign special statements that they were staying at their own risk.
Earlier on Sunday, a dyke crumbled on the German side of the Odra, south of Frankrurt flooding a village.

"Even though the floods are receding...and weather forecasts are optimistic, we are concered about the state of anti-flood dykes along the Odra and some other rivers. They are weak and soaked through like the sponge," Pomes said.
July's three-week-old flooding, the worst natural disaster in the region for centuries, killed 55 people in Poland, flooding 6,000 sq km of land and causing damages amounting to billions of dollars.
Pomes said that since Saturday water has retreated from some 200 sq km of land and about 1,900 sq km were under water.
People were returning to their homes, often to find debris, dead livestock, lack of fresh water and universal filth. More than 50,000 people were still displaced.
Many were complaining that the rescue and relief operations were chaotic and the police were not doing enough to stop looting in the flooded areas.

"Those who are stronger and also those who are less affected by the flood get more, because they have more time to scramble for aid. I can see no management," said pensioner Stanislawa Kislewska, from the southwestern village of Kotowice, one of more than 30 places still inundated.
Kislewska, who lost all her possessions -- a small house, 10 hens and 15 rabbits -- in the floods, could not hold back her tears.
"I do not know what I will do when all this ends, just as I did not know what to do when it began. Nobody told us what we should do," she told Reuters.
An opinion poll released over the weekend showed the majority of Poles were dissatisfied with the way the government had handled the flood crisis.
The government, which admits it was initially taken by surprise by the scale of the floods, has defended its actions.
It has approved a relief package which offers tax cuts, subsidised housing and investment loans as well as free distribution of food and medicine in the affected regions.
